The Oort Cloud. A hypothesized spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the solar system at vast distances—up to two hundred thousand astronomical units from the Sun, roughly one light-year away. Although never directly observed, the Oort Cloud is inferred from the trajectories of long-period comets and explains why comets with orbital periods of thousands of years approach Earth from random directions.

The Oort Cloud is named after Dutch astronomer Jan Oort, who in nineteen fifty proposed it to explain the origins of long-period comets and their apparent isotropic distribution in the sky. It lies far beyond Pluto and the Kuiper Belt, which ends around fifty astronomical units, at distances of two thousand to two hundred thousand astronomical units from the Sun, making it the outermost boundary of the solar system.

Comets in the Oort Cloud are thought to consist of volatile ices—water, methane, ammonia, and carbon dioxide—mixed with rock and dust. When a nearby star passes or galactic tides perturb orbits, they may be knocked inward toward the Sun. The Oort Cloud is not spherically symmetric. It has a denser inner region and a more diffuse outer zone, reflecting the complexity of planetary formation and gravitational scattering early in solar system history.

Comets arriving from the Oort Cloud have very high velocities and nearly random orbital inclinations, explaining why periodic comets like Halley's Comet, which returns every seventy-six years, come from much closer reservoirs like the Kuiper Belt. The cloud contains an estimated one to two trillion icy bodies, each larger than one kilometer—leftover planetesimals from the solar system's formation four point six billion years ago, ejected outward by interactions with the giant planets. The Oort Cloud is dynamically unstable on cosmic timescales: stellar encounters within the Milky Way slowly erode its outer boundary, and the cloud may have shed half its initial objects over the age of the solar system.
